blindSummary: This state/province applies religious criminal law as part of the twelve-jurisdiction bloc adopted by 2002. The religious layer criminalises conduct beyond the federal statute, including same-sex acts between women, with the death penalty on the statute book for men's 'sodomy'; the framework applies to adherents of the locally dominant faith, and its practical reach over visitors is mediated by arrest practice - including religious morality-police activity across the bloc - rather than by any formal 'tourists excepted' rule. No trans-specific incident or documented morality-police action appears for this state/province. Reporting-decay caveats apply: absence of records reflects fear of outing and surveillance gaps, not absence of risk.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation's report (2004) on the extension of religious criminal law: the first jurisdiction in the bloc enacted its religious-law establishment statute on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve jurisdictions had adopted some form of religious criminal law into their legislation - to date the only ones where religious courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

A foreign government's country-of-origin information note (June 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity: religious law derived from the locally dominant faith applies to its adherents in the twelve-jurisdiction bloc and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all twelve jurisdictions and penalties for acts between women range from death to flogging and imprisonment; includes a dedicated section on enforcement of the religious-law provisions and the practice of the religious morality-police force.
blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: a 2014 federal statute (up to 14 years, applies to visitors) plus the parallel religious-law penal layer for adherents of the locally dominant faith shape police and morality-police posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.
